topics.title: Views and View Controllers
topics.summary: UIView, the view hierarchy, frame and bounds, UIViewController: the building blocks everything else in UIKit rests on.

lesson.heading: Everything is a UIView
lesson.body:
In UIKit, everything you see on screen is a `UIView` or one of its subclasses: `UILabel`, `UIButton`, `UIImageView`, `UIScrollView`, `UIStackView`. A UIView is a rectangle that knows how to draw itself, receive touches, and contain other views.

The view doesn't draw on its own, though: every UIView owns a **CALayer** (`view.layer`), and the layer is what handles the actual drawing and animation. That's where `cornerRadius`, `borderWidth`, and `shadowOpacity` live. On top of the layer, the UIView adds touch event handling and Auto Layout integration.
lesson.code:
let box = UIView()
box.backgroundColor = .systemBlue
box.layer.cornerRadius = 12      // drawing goes through the layer

let label = UILabel()            // a label is a UIView too
label.text = "Hello"

lesson.heading: The view hierarchy
lesson.body:
Views form a **tree**: each one has a `superview` (its parent, optional) and an array of `subviews` (its children). You call `addSubview(_:)` on the parent, and it appends the child at the end; you call `removeFromSuperview()` on the child, and it detaches it from the tree.

The order of the `subviews` array is also the **drawing order**: later views draw on top. That's why the last view added is the one in front, and to change the order there's `bringSubviewToFront(_:)` and `insertSubview(_:at:)`.

The root of the tree is the `UIWindow`. If a view's `window` is `nil`, that view isn't on screen.
lesson.code:
container.addSubview(a)
container.addSubview(b)   // b draws ON TOP of a

container.subviews        // [a, b]
b.superview               // container

container.bringSubviewToFront(a)   // now a is in front
a.removeFromSuperview()            // called on the child

lesson.heading: frame, bounds, and center
lesson.body:
These are three ways of describing where a view is, and it's the most classic UIKit interview question.

- **`frame`**: the view's position and size in the **superview's** coordinate system.
- **`bounds`**: the same view seen from **its own** coordinate system. For a newly created view, `bounds.origin` is `(0, 0)` and the size matches the frame's.
- **`center`**: the center of the frame, also in the superview's coordinates.

The distinction matters in two cases. With a **transform** (a rotation, for example), `bounds` stays the same while `frame` becomes the rectangle that encloses the rotated view, so it's larger: with a non-identity transform, the frame is no longer reliable. And in a `UIScrollView`, scrolling moves `bounds.origin` (that's exactly what `contentOffset` is) while the frame stays put.
lesson.code:
let v = UIView(frame: CGRect(x: 40, y: 60, width: 100, height: 50))
v.frame     // (40, 60, 100, 50)  in the superview
v.bounds    // ( 0,  0, 100, 50)  in itself
v.center    // (90, 85)           in the superview

v.transform = CGAffineTransform(rotationAngle: .pi / 4)
v.bounds    // unchanged
v.frame     // larger: the box that encloses the rotated view

lesson.heading: UIViewController: who owns the screen
lesson.body:
A `UIViewController` manages a screen, or a portion of one. Its interface lives in the **`view`** property, the local root of the tree: everything the controller shows is a subview of it.

The `view` is **lazy**: it doesn't exist at the end of `init`, it's created the first time someone accesses the property. That's why `@IBOutlet`s are `nil` inside init and only set from `viewDidLoad` onward, and also why reading `self.view` too early can load the interface sooner than expected.

Controllers nest inside each other: a `UINavigationController` or a `UITabBarController` is a **container**, and the controllers it shows are its `children`.

lesson.heading: Building the interface: code, XIB, or Storyboard
lesson.body:
There are three approaches, and you can mix them freely.

- **In code**: you create the views in `viewDidLoad` (or in `loadView` if you want to replace the root view) and constrain them by hand. Verbose but explicit, and it diffs cleanly in code review.
- **XIB**: one file for a single view or a single controller.
- **Storyboard**: several screens together, connected by `segue`s.

With XIBs and Storyboards, view references are declared as `@IBOutlet` and actions as `@IBAction`. The connections are resolved when the file loads: if you rename or disconnect an outlet without updating the nib, the app crashes when the screen opens with the classic *"this class is not key value coding-compliant"*.

Rule of thumb: `override func loadView()` is for **creating** the root view and must not call `super` if you assign it yourself; `viewDidLoad` is for **configuring** it and must always call `super`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a subclass of UIView?
questions.explanation: `UIViewController` isn't a view: it's a controller, and it inherits from `UIResponder`. It owns a view in its `view` property, but it isn't one. Labels, stack views, and image views, on the other hand, are all subclasses of `UIView`.
whyWrong: `UILabel` is a full-fledged UIView: you add it to the hierarchy with `addSubview`, it has a frame, and it draws text.
`UIStackView` is a special UIView (it draws nothing of its own and lays out its arrangedSubviews), but it's still a subclass of UIView.
`UIImageView` is the UIView specialized in drawing a `UIImage`: it has a frame, bounds, and a superview like any other.

questions.prompt: Which view is in front after this code?
options: b, because it was added last
a, because it was added first
It depends on their zPosition, which is the same here
questions.explanation: `addSubview` appends to the end of the `subviews` array, and that array is also the drawing order: later views draw on top. So `b` covers `a`. To swap them, use `bringSubviewToFront(a)` or `insertSubview(a, aboveSubview: b)`.
whyWrong: It's the other way around: the first one added ends up at the bottom of the stack. The `subviews` array is drawn from first to last, so the last one wins.
`zPosition` exists on the layer and can override the order, but it hasn't been touched here: with equal zPosition, the order in `subviews` decides.
The overlap is clean, not partial: `b` is drawn entirely on top of `a` wherever the two frames intersect.

questions.prompt: What is `v.bounds.origin`?
questions.code: let v = UIView(frame: CGRect(x: 40, y: 60, width: 100, height: 50))
questions.explanation: `bounds` describes the view in **its own** coordinate system, which always starts at zero for a newly created view. It's the `frame` that is `(40, 60, 100, 50)`, because it positions the view inside the superview.
whyWrong: (40, 60) is the origin of the **frame**, meaning the position in the superview. Bounds looks at the view from the inside and starts at zero.
(90, 85) is the `center`, the midpoint of the frame: 40 + 100/2 and 60 + 50/2. It's not an origin.
(100, 50) is the **size**, which lives in `bounds.size` (and `frame.size`), not in `bounds.origin`.

questions.prompt: How do you remove a view from the hierarchy?
options: By calling `removeFromSuperview()` on the view to remove
questions.explanation: `removeFromSuperview()` is called on the **child**, unlike `addSubview(_:)`, which is called on the parent. It's the only one of the four that actually exists.
whyWrong: `removeSubview(_:)` doesn't exist in UIKit: the asymmetry with `addSubview(_:)` often trips people up, but removal goes through the child.
`superview` is a **read-only** property: you change the hierarchy with methods, not by assigning the parent by hand.
`frame` is a `CGRect`, not an optional: it can't be `nil`. And zeroing it out would just make the view invisible while leaving it in the tree.

questions.prompt: Where does the interface managed by a UIViewController live?
options: In its `view` property, the root of all the others
Directly in the `UIWindow`, with nothing in between
questions.explanation: Every `UIViewController` owns a root view in its `view` property: everything the screen shows is a subview of it. The controller isn't a view and has neither `subviews` nor a `layer`.
whyWrong: The window is the root of the whole app, not of a single screen: between the window and the content there's always the controller's `view`.
`subviews` is a property of `UIView`, not `UIViewController`. The screen's subviews are in `controller.view.subviews`.
`layer` belongs to `UIView`. From the controller you get there through the view: `controller.view.layer`.

questions.prompt: You rotate a view 45 degrees with a transform. What happens to frame and bounds?
questions.code: v.transform = CGAffineTransform(rotationAngle: .pi / 4)
options: Bounds stays the same, frame becomes the box that encloses the rotated view
Frame stays the same, bounds grows
Neither changes: the transform only affects drawing
questions.explanation: `bounds` is the view as seen from itself, and rotation doesn't touch it. `frame`, instead, is the **axis-aligned** rectangle that encloses the view in the superview, so it grows when the view rotates. Hence the rule: with a non-identity transform, the frame is no longer a value you can do math with.
whyWrong: Only the frame changes: bounds describes the view in its own coordinate system, which rotates along with it and therefore stays the same.
It's exactly the opposite: bounds is the one immune to rotation, frame is the one that grows to enclose the rotated view.
The transform really does change the reported geometry: reading `v.frame` after a rotation returns the new enclosing box, not the old one.

questions.prompt: When is a UIViewController's `view` created?
options: The first time the `view` property is accessed
Only if the controller comes from a Storyboard
questions.explanation: The `view` is loaded **lazily**: `loadView()` and then `viewDidLoad()` fire on the first access to the property. That's why `@IBOutlet`s are `nil` in init, and why touching `self.view` too early forces the screen to load ahead of time.
whyWrong: When `init` returns, the view doesn't exist yet: that's precisely why interface setup belongs in `viewDidLoad` and not in the initializer.
On deallocation the view is released, if anything, not created. Loading happens at the start of the controller's life, not the end.
Lazy loading works the same way for Storyboards, XIBs, and code: only *how* the view is built inside `loadView()` changes.

questions.prompt: Why is an `@IBOutlet` `nil` inside the view controller's `init`?
options: Because outlets are connected when the view loads, which happens after init
Because outlets are always `weak` and die immediately without strong references
Because `private` prevents the nib from writing to them
Because the label hasn't been added to a superview yet
questions.explanation: The nib or storyboard is deserialized inside `loadView()`, which fires on the first access to `view`, that is, after `init`. That's when the outlets get connected, and they're usable from `viewDidLoad` onward.
whyWrong: A `weak` outlet still stays alive as long as the view is in the hierarchy, which retains it. The problem is *when*, not the strength of the reference.
`private` limits visibility in Swift but doesn't block the connection: the nib uses the Objective-C runtime's key-value coding, which is why `@IBOutlet` alone makes it reachable.
The nib's label is born already inside the file's hierarchy. But in init that file hasn't been loaded yet, so the label doesn't exist at all.

questions.prompt: In a UIScrollView, what changes when you scroll the content down by 100 points?
options: `bounds.origin.y` increases by 100: that's exactly what `contentOffset` is
Nothing in the scroll view's geometry: only its subviews move
questions.explanation: A scroll view doesn't move its content: it moves the **window** it looks through, meaning its own `bounds.origin`. `contentOffset` is just another name for that point. The `frame` stays put, because the scroll view always occupies the same space in its superview.
whyWrong: The frame is the scroll view's position **inside its superview**, and scrolling doesn't move it a single pixel: it stays where it is, only what it shows changes.
The `center` is derived from the frame, so it stays put too. Scrolling happens entirely in the internal coordinate system.
The geometry definitely changes: it's `bounds.origin` that moves, which is why the subviews appear to scroll even though their frames stay constant.

questions.prompt: What actually draws a UIView's content?
options: Its `CALayer`: the UIView adds touches and layout on top
The UIView itself; the layer is only for animations
The `UIWindow`, which draws for every view in the tree
questions.explanation: Every UIView owns a `CALayer` (`view.layer`), and Core Animation handles drawing and compositing. The UIView is a wrapper that adds touch event handling, Auto Layout, and the responder chain. That's why `cornerRadius`, `borderWidth`, and `shadowPath` live on the layer.
whyWrong: The layer isn't just for animating: it's what holds the drawn content (the backing store) and composites it on screen, animations or not.
The window is the root of the tree and doesn't draw on behalf of its children: each view contributes its own layer, and Core Animation composites them.
The controller coordinates, it doesn't draw: it has neither a layer nor any graphical content of its own.

topics.title: View Lifecycle
topics.summary: From loadView to viewDidDisappear, all the way to the app and scene lifecycle.

lesson.heading: The full sequence
lesson.body:
When a view controller is shown for the first time, UIKit calls, in order: `loadView`, `viewDidLoad`, `viewWillAppear`, `viewIsAppearing`, `viewWillLayoutSubviews`/`viewDidLayoutSubviews` (possibly several times), and finally `viewDidAppear`. On the way out come `viewWillDisappear` and `viewDidDisappear`.

**viewDidLoad is called only once** per view load: it's the place for one-time setup (subviews, constraints, bindings). The other appearance methods can be called many times.

lesson.heading: loadView and lazy loading
lesson.body:
A view controller's view is **lazy**: it's created only on the first access to `view`, which triggers `loadView` and then `viewDidLoad`. You override `loadView` only to create the root view in code: in that case you assign `self.view` and do **not** call `super`.

Never call `loadView` directly: use `loadViewIfNeeded()`, and check the state with `isViewLoaded`. Before the view loads, `@IBOutlet`s are still `nil`.

lesson.heading: Layout and geometry
lesson.body:
In `viewDidLoad` the view doesn't have its final size yet: `bounds` may reflect the nib or the default screen size. Size-dependent code belongs in `viewDidLayoutSubviews` (which must be idempotent, since it's called often) or, better yet, expressed with constraints.

Since iOS 17 (back-deployed to iOS 13) there's `viewIsAppearing`: called once per appearance, after `viewWillAppear`, when the view is already in the hierarchy with an up-to-date trait collection and geometry.

lesson.heading: Modal presentations and containment
lesson.body:
With the default `.pageSheet` style (iOS 13+), the presenter stays visible beneath the sheet, so it **doesn't receive** `viewWillDisappear`/`viewDidDisappear` when the sheet opens, or `viewWillAppear` when it closes. With `.fullScreen` it does: this is a classic source of refresh bugs.

For child view controllers, the correct sequence is `addChild`, `addSubview`, and `didMove(toParent:)`; to remove them, `willMove(toParent: nil)`, `removeFromSuperview`, and `removeFromParent`. That way appearance events are forwarded correctly.
lesson.code:
addChild(child)
view.addSubview(child.view)
child.didMove(toParent: self)

lesson.heading: App and scene lifecycle
lesson.body:
Since iOS 13, with scenes, the `AppDelegate` handles process-level events (`didFinishLaunchingWithOptions`, scene configuration, push tokens), while the `SceneDelegate` handles the UI: `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)` creates the `UIWindow`, followed by `sceneWillEnterForeground`, `sceneDidBecomeActive`, `sceneWillResignActive`, and `sceneDidEnterBackground`.

The app states are **not running, inactive, active, background, suspended**. With scenes enabled, the `AppDelegate`'s foreground/background methods are no longer called.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Typical question: **"What's the difference between viewDidLoad and viewWillAppear?"** Short answer: `viewDidLoad` happens once, when the view is loaded into memory, and it's for setup; `viewWillAppear` happens every time the view appears, and it's for refreshing data or UI. Add that the final geometry only arrives with layout (`viewDidLayoutSubviews` or `viewIsAppearing`), and bring up the `.pageSheet` case, which shows real-world experience.

questions.prompt: Which method is called **only once** per load of a view controller's view?
questions.explanation: `viewDidLoad` follows `loadView` and happens once per load; the others can repeat on every appearance or layout pass.
whyWrong: `viewWillAppear` sounds like initialization, but it's called **on every appearance**, for example every time you come back to this VC with a pop.
Careful: `viewDidLayoutSubviews` fires on **every layout pass** (rotation, size change, `setNeedsLayout`), so it can repeat many times.
`viewDidAppear` arrives every time the view appears, not just once: if the screen gets covered and then uncovered, it's called again.

questions.prompt: In what order are the logs printed the first time this view controller is presented?
questions.explanation: The view is first created (`loadView`), then configured (`viewDidLoad`); layout happens between `viewWillAppear` and `viewDidAppear`.
whyWrong: `viewDidLoad` can't come before `loadView`: it's `loadView` that creates the view, and only then does UIKit call `viewDidLoad` to configure it.
Layout doesn't happen before `viewWillAppear`: the view is inserted into the hierarchy after that callback, and only then does `viewDidLayoutSubviews` arrive.
This puts D after E, but the first layout pass is required before the view becomes visible: `viewDidLayoutSubviews` comes before `viewDidAppear`.

questions.prompt: Why can reading `view.bounds.width` in `viewDidLoad` give the wrong value?
options: The view hasn't been created yet
Layout hasn't happened yet: the size isn't final
questions.explanation: In `viewDidLoad` the view exists but has the nib's or the default size; you get the real geometry after the layout pass.
whyWrong: It's not necessarily zero: in `viewDidLoad`, `bounds` already has a size, the nib's or the screen's; it's just **not the final one yet**.
`viewDidLoad` runs on the **main thread**, like every UIKit callback; the problem is layout timing, not threading.
The view already exists: `viewDidLoad` comes right after `loadView`. The value is wrong because layout hasn't happened yet.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run this code before presenting `vc`, when `titleLabel` is an `@IBOutlet` from a storyboard?
questions.code:
let vc = storyboard.instantiateViewController(
    identifier: "Detail") as! DetailViewController
vc.titleLabel.text = "Hello"
present(vc, animated: true)
options: Crash: the outlet is still `nil` because the view isn't loaded
questions.explanation: Outlets are connected only when the view loads: it's better to pass the data in a property and apply it in `viewDidLoad`.
whyWrong: It's tempting to think so, but `instantiateViewController` only creates the VC: outlets are connected when the view loads, so here they're still `nil`.
An `@IBOutlet` is implicitly unwrapped (`UILabel!`): accessing it while it's `nil` isn't ignored, it causes a **crash**.
UIKit doesn't defer the assignment: the line runs immediately, finds the outlet `nil`, and the app crashes before it even reaches `present`.

questions.prompt: VC A presents B with the default style on iOS 17. Which statement is true for A?
options: It receives both, just like with a push
It receives `viewDidDisappear` only if B is animated
questions.explanation: The `.automatic` style resolves to `.pageSheet` and A stays visible: no disappear callbacks, and no `viewWillAppear` on dismissal.
whyWrong: There's no middle ground: with `.pageSheet`, A stays visible beneath the sheet, so UIKit sends **neither** of the two disappear callbacks.
A push fully replaces A's view, a sheet doesn't: with `.automatic` → `.pageSheet`, A stays in the hierarchy and receives no callbacks.
Animation has nothing to do with it: what matters is the presentation style. With `.pageSheet`, A stays visible and `viewDidDisappear` doesn't arrive either way.

questions.prompt: In a scene-based app (iOS 13+), where do you typically create the `UIWindow` in code?
questions.explanation: With scenes, every window belongs to a `UIWindowScene`, created when the scene connects.
whyWrong: That was the right place before iOS 13; with scenes, the `AppDelegate` no longer manages windows, which belong to a `UIWindowScene`.
The root VC lives **inside** the window: it can't create it, because a window has to exist already in order to show it.
`sceneDidBecomeActive` can be called many times (every return to the foreground): creating the window there would recreate it every time.

questions.prompt: What's missing from this containment code?
questions.code:
let child = MapViewController()
addChild(child)
view.addSubview(child.view)
child.view.frame = view.bounds
questions.explanation: `addChild` already calls `willMove(toParent:)`, but `didMove(toParent:)` has to be called manually after adding the view.
whyWrong: Not needed: `addChild(_:)` already calls `willMove(toParent:)` automatically. What you have to do by hand is `didMove(toParent:)`.
`loadView()` should never be called directly: accessing `child.view` is already enough to load the child's view.
It looks complete, but without `didMove(toParent: self)` the child is never told that the containment transition has finished.

questions.prompt: When is `viewIsAppearing(_:)` called?
options: Between `viewWillAppear` and `viewDidAppear`, once geometry is ready
Only when the trait collection changes
questions.explanation: Introduced in iOS 17 and available back to iOS 13, it's the ideal spot for updates that depend on size and traits, once per appearance.
whyWrong: It arrives **after** `viewWillAppear` and on every appearance, not just once: it exists precisely so that geometry is already in place.
It doesn't follow `viewDidAppear` and doesn't repeat on every layout pass: it's called once per appearance, before the transition finishes.
Trait changes have their own APIs (`registerForTraitChanges`); `viewIsAppearing` is tied to the view appearing.

questions.prompt: The user presses Home while the app is active (scene-based app). In what order do the callbacks arrive?
questions.explanation: The scene first goes from active to inactive and then moves to the background; `sceneDidDisconnect` happens only if the system discards the scene.
whyWrong: Wrong order: the scene first has to stop being active (`sceneWillResignActive`) and only then moves to the background.
In a scene-based app, state callbacks go to the `SceneDelegate`: `applicationDidEnterBackground` isn't the only one, and it often goes unused.
Pressing Home doesn't disconnect the scene: `sceneDidDisconnect` happens only if the system discards it to free up resources.

questions.prompt: What's the correct way to override `loadView` to use a custom view?
options: Assign `view` in `init` and leave the override empty
questions.explanation: `super.loadView()` looks for a nib or creates an empty `UIView`: wasted work if you're going to replace it anyway.
whyWrong: It works, but `super.loadView()` creates an empty `UIView` (or loads a nib) just so you can put your view inside it: wasted work and an extra view.
`loadView()` should never be called by hand, and in `viewDidLoad` the view already exists: UIKit calls `loadView` when it needs to.
Assigning `view` in `init` forces loading too early, and an empty `loadView` leaves `view` as `nil` if you haven't already set it.

topics.title: Auto Layout
topics.summary: Constraints, priorities, hugging, compression resistance, stack views, and the layout cycle.

lesson.heading: Constraints as equations
lesson.body:
Every constraint is a linear equation: `item1.attr = multiplier × item2.attr + constant`, with a `==`, `<=`, or `>=` relation. The layout must be **unambiguous** (exactly one solution) and **satisfiable** (no conflicts).

For views created in code, set `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false`; otherwise UIKit generates constraints from the autoresizing mask that conflict with yours. Activate constraints in bulk with `NSLayoutConstraint.activate`.
lesson.code:
label.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    label.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
    label.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor, constant: -16),
    label.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor)
])

lesson.heading: Priorities
lesson.body:
Priorities range from 1 to 1000; `1000` (`.required`) must be satisfied. An optional constraint that can't be met is satisfied as closely as possible. If two required constraints conflict, Auto Layout **breaks** one of them at runtime and logs "Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints" (symbolic breakpoint `UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints`).

Careful: you can't switch an already installed constraint from required to non-required (or vice versa): create it with priority 999 from the start.

lesson.heading: intrinsicContentSize, hugging, and compression resistance
lesson.body:
Controls like `UILabel`, `UIButton`, and `UIImageView` have an `intrinsicContentSize` that generates implicit constraints. **Content hugging** = resistance to growing larger than the content; **compression resistance** = resistance to shrinking smaller than it.

With two labels side by side, the one with the lower hugging priority stretches, and the one with the lower compression resistance gets truncated. In custom views, call `invalidateIntrinsicContentSize()` whenever the content changes.
lesson.code:
titleLabel.setContentHuggingPriority(.defaultHigh, for: .horizontal)
valueLabel.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.required, for: .horizontal)

lesson.heading: UIStackView
lesson.body:
`UIStackView` generates the constraints for its `arrangedSubviews` based on `axis`, `distribution`, `alignment`, and `spacing`. Setting `isHidden = true` on an arranged subview removes it from the layout, and the others take up its space (animatable).

Use `addArrangedSubview`, not `addSubview`. Since iOS 14, stack views also render `backgroundColor`; before that they were a non-rendering layer.

lesson.heading: The layout cycle
lesson.body:
A layout pass has three phases: **update constraints**, **layout** (`layoutSubviews`), and **display** (`draw(_:)`). `setNeedsLayout()` marks the view as needing an update on the next run loop cycle (asynchronous, cheap); `layoutIfNeeded()` performs layout immediately if there are pending changes.

To animate a constraint, change its `constant` outside the animation and call `layoutIfNeeded()` on the superview inside the block.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Typical question: **"What's the difference between content hugging and compression resistance?"** Short answer: both act on the `intrinsicContentSize`; hugging keeps a view from growing, compression resistance keeps it from shrinking; between two views, the higher priority wins. Then give a concrete example (two labels in a row) and bring up `setNeedsLayout` vs `layoutIfNeeded` for animations.

questions.prompt: Two labels in a row fill the horizontal space. Which one stretches?
questions.code:
left.setContentHuggingPriority(.init(251), for: .horizontal)
right.setContentHuggingPriority(.init(250), for: .horizontal)
options: Neither: the layout is ambiguous and crashes
questions.explanation: Lower hugging means less resistance to growing: that's the view that absorbs the extra space.
whyWrong: Higher hugging is resistance to **growing**: `left` at 251 "hugs" its content and stays narrow, so the other one grows.
With different hugging priorities there's no tie: Auto Layout grows only the view with the lower hugging.
Different priorities exist precisely to remove ambiguity; and an ambiguous layout doesn't crash anyway, it just gives an unpredictable result.

questions.prompt: You add constraints to a view created in code, but the console reports conflicts with `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint`. What's the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: With the flag set to `true`, UIKit creates constraints from the frame/autoresizing mask, and they conflict with your explicit ones.
whyWrong: `NSLayoutConstraint.activate` and `isActive = true` are equivalent: neither one generates autoresizing constraints.
A missing `intrinsicContentSize` can make the layout ambiguous, but it doesn't produce `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint` constraints.
Priorities of 1000 can cause conflicts among your own constraints, but `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint` constraints only come from leaving the flag at `true`.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
options: The view animates correctly over 0.3 s
Crash: constraints can't be modified inside an animation
No animation: the view jumps on the next layout pass
questions.explanation: Changing `constant` doesn't animate anything: you need `layoutIfNeeded()` inside the block so the frames change during the animation.
whyWrong: It seems natural, but changing `constant` only updates the constraint model: the frames change at layout time, outside the animation block.
No crash: modifying a constraint inside `animate` is perfectly legal. It's just missing `layoutIfNeeded()` to animate the frames.
`viewDidAppear` has nothing to do with it: the animation isn't deferred, there's simply nothing to animate in the block.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `setNeedsLayout()` and `layoutIfNeeded()`?
options: The first runs immediately, the second on the next cycle
The first marks for the next cycle, the second runs immediately
The first updates constraints, the second redraws
questions.explanation: `setNeedsLayout` is asynchronous and coalesces requests; `layoutIfNeeded` forces a synchronous layout if there are pending changes.
whyWrong: They aren't equivalent: one just flags the view as needing layout, the other performs layout **right away**, synchronously.
The behavior is reversed: `setNeedsLayout` defers to the next cycle, `layoutIfNeeded` runs immediately.
You're thinking of `setNeedsUpdateConstraints` and `setNeedsDisplay`: both methods in the question are about layout, not drawing.

questions.prompt: Two labels don't fit in the row. Which one gets truncated?
questions.code:
name.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.init(750), for: .horizontal)
price.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.init(751), for: .horizontal)
options: Neither: it runs off the screen
questions.explanation: Lower compression resistance means less resistance to shrinking: that label gives way and shows the ellipsis.
whyWrong: Higher compression resistance means `price` **resists** shrinking: it's the other label that gives way.
With different priorities there's no proportional split: only the view with the lower compression resistance gives way.
Auto Layout tries to honor the required constraints to the edges, sacrificing the lower priority: `name` gets truncated, it doesn't run off the screen.

questions.prompt: What happens when you run this line on an already active constraint created with required priority?
questions.code: widthConstraint.priority = .defaultHigh   // from 1000 to 750
options: The priority changes and the layout updates
An exception is raised at runtime
questions.explanation: Switching an installed constraint from required to optional isn't supported: create it with 999 if you'll need to change it.
whyWrong: The change would be legal between two optional priorities, but switching an installed constraint from required (1000) to optional isn't supported.
UIKit doesn't silently ignore it: this transition violates an internal assertion and raises an exception.
Changing the priority doesn't deactivate the constraint (that takes `isActive = false`); what you get here is an exception.

questions.prompt: In a `UIStackView`, you set `isHidden = true` on an arranged subview. What happens?
options: It becomes transparent but still takes up space
It leaves the layout and the others take up its space
questions.explanation: The stack view observes `isHidden` and recalculates the layout; the view stays in `arrangedSubviews`.
whyWrong: That's what happens with `alpha = 0`: with `isHidden = true` the stack view removes the view from the layout and the others take up its space.
The view stays in `arrangedSubviews`: the stack view just skips it when computing the layout, as long as `isHidden` is `true`.
No ambiguity: the stack view manages its own constraints and recalculates the arrangement without the hidden view.

questions.prompt: A custom view computes its `intrinsicContentSize` from its text. After changing the text, the size doesn't update. What's missing?
questions.explanation: Auto Layout caches the intrinsic size: you have to invalidate it explicitly when the content changes.
whyWrong: `setNeedsDisplay()` only asks for the content to be redrawn with `draw(_:)`: it doesn't tell Auto Layout that the intrinsic size has changed.
`sizeToFit()` resizes the frame of whatever receives it, here the superview, and doesn't invalidate your view's cached intrinsic size.
Setting the flag back to `true` generates constraints from the frame that conflict with the others; the intrinsic size would still be cached anyway.

questions.prompt: What does Auto Layout do at runtime if two required constraints conflict?
options: It breaks one of the constraints and logs a warning to the console
It crashes immediately with an exception
It ignores all of the view's constraints
It always uses the last constraint added, without logging
questions.explanation: The system picks a constraint to break so it can satisfy the others, and logs it; the app keeps running, but the layout may be wrong.
whyWrong: No crash: the conflict is resolved by breaking a constraint and logging "Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints".
The engine doesn't throw everything away: it gives up **one** constraint and tries to honor all the others.
The order in which constraints are added decides nothing, and the system always logs to the console when it breaks a constraint.

questions.prompt: The superview is 320 pt wide. How wide will `box` be?
options: Ambiguous: it depends on the order
questions.explanation: The required constraint caps it at 280; the optional one at 300 can't be satisfied, so it's met as closely as possible.
whyWrong: 300 pt would be honored only if the limit allowed it, but the required constraint caps it at 320 − 40 = 280 pt.
The superview's width comes in with `constant: -40` and `lessThanOrEqualTo`: it can't reach 320.
Different priorities (750 vs. required) leave no ambiguity: the required constraint wins, and the other is satisfied as closely as possible.

topics.title: Table and Collection Views
topics.summary: Cell reuse, data sources, diffable, compositional layout, and prefetching.

lesson.heading: Data source and delegate
lesson.body:
`UITableView` and `UICollectionView` split responsibilities: the **data source** supplies the data (`numberOfRowsInSection`, `cellForRowAt`), and the **delegate** handles behavior and appearance (`didSelectRowAt`, `willDisplay`, heights).

The model must always match what the view thinks it's showing: inserting rows with `insertRows` without updating the array first crashes with `NSInternalInconsistencyException`.

lesson.heading: Cell reuse
lesson.body:
Cells are recycled: only the visible ones exist, plus a few in the reuse queue. You register a class or nib and call `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)`, which crashes if the identifier isn't registered.

Golden rule: in `cellForRowAt`, **set all of the cell's state**, because it may arrive carrying another row's data. In `prepareForReuse`, reset transient state and cancel async tasks, such as an image download.

lesson.heading: Diffable data source
lesson.body:
Since iOS 13, `UITableViewDiffableDataSource` and `UICollectionViewDiffableDataSource` replace manual index path bookkeeping: you build an `NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot` with unique `Hashable` identifiers, then call `apply`, which computes the differences and animates them.

To update the content of an existing item, use `reconfigureItems` (iOS 15), which reconfigures the existing cell instead of dequeuing a new one the way `reloadItems` does.
lesson.code:
var snapshot = NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<Section, Item.ID>()
snapshot.appendSections([.main])
snapshot.appendItems(items.map(\.id))
dataSource.apply(snapshot, animatingDifferences: true)

lesson.heading: Compositional layout
lesson.body:
`UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout` describes the layout as **item → group → section**, with `fractionalWidth`, `absolute`, or `estimated` dimensions. Each section can have its own layout, and `orthogonalScrollingBehavior` gives you horizontal carousels without nested collection views.

It's the modern alternative to `UICollectionViewFlowLayout` and to custom `UICollectionViewLayout` subclasses.

lesson.heading: Prefetching and performance
lesson.body:
With `UITableViewDataSourcePrefetching` you get `prefetchRowsAt` for upcoming rows and `cancelPrefetchingForRowsAt` for rows that are no longer needed. Prefetching is a hint: `cellForRowAt` must still be able to load the data on its own.

Avoid heavy work in `cellForRowAt` (parsing, image decoding, creating formatters every time). For self-sizing cells, use `UITableView.automaticDimension` with a reasonable estimate.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Classic question: **"Why does a list sometimes show the wrong image in a cell?"** Short answer: because of reuse, the download finishes when the cell is already showing a different row. You fix it by canceling the task in `prepareForReuse` and checking that the row's identifier is still the same before assigning the image. Wrap up by mentioning diffable data sources and `reconfigureItems` as the modern approach.

questions.prompt: Why does `UITableView` reuse cells?
options: To preserve cell state across scrolls
To limit memory and allocations to just the visible cells
questions.explanation: Allocating a cell for every row would be expensive: only the visible ones stay alive, plus a small reuse queue.
whyWrong: Reuse does the opposite: a reused cell carries over the previous row's state, which is exactly why you have to reconfigure it every time.
Cells can be deallocated just fine; reuse is an efficiency choice, not a constraint.
Insertion animations exist regardless of reuse: the reason is to limit allocations and memory to the visible cells.

questions.prompt: When scrolling fast, some cells briefly show another row's image. Why?
options: The download finishes after the cell has already been reused
questions.explanation: The captured cell may be showing a different row by the time the response arrives: cancel the task in `prepareForReuse` or verify identity.
whyWrong: `dequeue` isn't random: it returns a cell from the reuse queue, but that cell may have been used by another row.
The closure runs once per request; the problem is that it writes to a cell that **in the meantime** is showing a different row.
Moving the assignment to `willDisplay` doesn't fix it: the async download can still land after the cell has been reused.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run only this line without changing the `items` array?
questions.code:
tableView.insertRows(at: [IndexPath(row: 0, section: 0)],
                     with: .automatic)
questions.explanation: The table checks that the row count after the update equals the previous count plus the insertions: the data source doesn't add up, so the app crashes.
whyWrong: The table doesn't conjure cells out of nothing: it compares the row count before and after, and if it doesn't match the data source, it throws an exception.
UIKit doesn't ignore the inconsistency: it checks that `numberOfRows` equals the previous rows plus the insertions, and crashes otherwise.
`insertRows` doesn't turn into `reloadData()`: with an unchanged data source, the consistency check fails and the app crashes.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)` with an identifier that was never registered?
options: It returns the first registered cell
An exception is raised and the app crashes
questions.explanation: The `for:` variant always returns a non-optional cell, so without registration it raises an exception.
whyWrong: That's what the old variant without `for:` does, returning an optional: the `for:` variant returns a non-optional cell and crashes.
UIKit doesn't make up a default cell: without registration it doesn't know which class or nib to use, so it raises an exception.
There's no fallback to the first registered cell: every identifier must be registered, or the app crashes.

questions.prompt: What requirement must the item identifiers in a diffable snapshot meet?
options: Be `Hashable` and unique within the snapshot
questions.explanation: Diffing relies on hashing; duplicate identifiers cause an error when you apply the snapshot.
whyWrong: `Codable` is for serialization, but diffing relies on hashing and equality: the requirement is `Hashable`.
Identifiers can be any `Hashable` type, including `UUID` or strings; they don't need to be integers, let alone consecutive ones.
Structs and enums work perfectly well: identity comes from `Hashable`, not from being a reference type.

questions.prompt: What's the advantage of `reconfigureItems` over `reloadItems` on a diffable snapshot?
options: It updates the existing cell without dequeuing a new one
It recomputes the entire collection layout
It also works with non-`Hashable` identifiers
It doesn't require applying the snapshot
questions.explanation: `reloadItems` replaces the cell with a new one; `reconfigureItems` (iOS 15) reruns the configuration on the already visible cell, which is more efficient.
whyWrong: `reconfigureItems` acts on the specific cells you pass it; it doesn't redo the layout of the whole collection.
Every identifier in a diffable snapshot must be `Hashable`, including for `reconfigureItems`.
You still have to `apply` the snapshot: `reconfigureItems` only marks the items, and the update happens when you apply.

questions.prompt: What's the correct hierarchy of a compositional layout?
questions.explanation: Items live in groups, groups make up a section, and sections compose the layout.
whyWrong: The section contains the groups, not the other way around: you start from the bottom, with items, the smallest elements.
A group is a container of items, so the item comes before the group, not after.
An item doesn't go directly into a section: it has to live in a group, which in turn forms the section.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `prefetchRowsAt` is correct?
options: It's called for every row before `cellForRowAt`
It always runs on a background thread
It isn't guaranteed: `cellForRowAt` must load the data on its own
questions.explanation: Prefetching is an optimization the system can skip, for example during very fast scrolling.
whyWrong: Prefetching is neither guaranteed nor systematic: the system can skip it, for example during very fast scrolling.
It doesn't replace anything: `cellForRowAt` is still required and must work even if the prefetch never happened.
`prefetchRowsAt` is called on the **main thread**; it's up to you to move heavy work to the background.

questions.prompt: What's appropriate to do in `prepareForReuse()`?
options: Configure the cell with the new row's data
Reset transient state and cancel async tasks
Remove all subviews and recreate them
questions.explanation: The new row's data belongs in `cellForRowAt`; `prepareForReuse` is for cleaning up whatever the previous row left behind.
whyWrong: Configuring with the new data belongs in `cellForRowAt`, where you know the `IndexPath`: in `prepareForReuse` you don't yet know which row is coming.
Recreating subviews on every reuse defeats the purpose of reuse: resetting state is enough, no need to rebuild the hierarchy.
Calling `reloadData()` from a cell would restart reuse for every cell: you risk loops and a huge amount of work on every scroll.

questions.prompt: A self-sizing cell expands its text after a tap, but its height doesn't change. How do you force a recalculation without reloading the cell?
questions.explanation: An empty batch update (or `beginUpdates`/`endUpdates`) recalculates heights with animation, without dequeuing again.
whyWrong: `setNeedsDisplay()` only redraws the cell's content: the table doesn't recalculate row heights.
`layoutIfNeeded()` lays out the table's subviews again, but doesn't make it query row heights again.
With `rowHeight` set to 0 the rows collapse: self-sizing cells need `UITableView.automaticDimension`, not 0.

topics.title: Navigation
topics.summary: Navigation stack, modals, segues vs. code, coordinators, and passing data back.

lesson.heading: UINavigationController
lesson.body:
It manages a **stack** of view controllers: `pushViewController` adds one, `popViewController` removes one, and `setViewControllers` replaces the whole stack. The stack holds VCs strongly: once a VC is removed, it should deallocate.

The back button title belongs to the **previous** VC: you set it on the `navigationItem.backButtonTitle` of the VC doing the push, not the one being shown.

lesson.heading: Modal presentation
lesson.body:
`present(_:animated:)` shows a VC modally. On iPhone since iOS 13, the default `.automatic` style resolves to `.pageSheet`, which can be dismissed with a swipe; to block that, set `isModalInPresentation = true`. `.fullScreen` removes the presenter's view from the hierarchy, while `.overFullScreen` keeps it (useful for transparent backgrounds).

`dismiss(animated:)` can be called from the presented VC: UIKit forwards the request to the presenter. A VC can present only one VC at a time.

lesson.heading: Segues or navigation in code
lesson.body:
With storyboards, you pass data in `prepare(for:sender:)` and go back with **unwind segues**. Navigation in code is more explicit and testable, and enables **dependency injection** through `init`.

Since iOS 13, `instantiateViewController(identifier:creator:)` enables injection with storyboards too, using a custom `init?(coder:)`.

lesson.heading: Coordinator pattern
lesson.body:
A **coordinator** owns the navigation logic: it creates the VCs, configures them, and decides where to go next. VCs don't know about each other and report actions through delegates or closures, so they're reusable.

Child coordinators are kept in an array and removed when their flow ends. The tricky part is the system back button: you intercept it with `UINavigationControllerDelegate` in `didShow`, checking the `transitionCoordinator`'s source VC.

lesson.heading: Passing data back
lesson.body:
The classic options are: a **delegate** (protocol constrained to `AnyObject`, `weak` property), a callback **closure** (with `[weak self]`), `NotificationCenter` for one-to-many communication, and Combine publishers.

Going forward, you use init injection or property injection before the push or present.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Classic question: **"How do you pass data from a child VC back to the previous one?"** Short answer: a weak delegate or a closure, depending on whether you have many related callbacks or just one. Mention that the protocol must be class-bound to allow `weak`, and that in large apps navigation should be pulled out into a coordinator to decouple the VCs.

questions.prompt: On iPhone with iOS 13+, which presentation style do you get with the default `.automatic`?
questions.explanation: Since iOS 13, `.automatic` almost always resolves to `.pageSheet`, which can be dismissed by swiping down.
whyWrong: `.fullScreen` was the behavior before iOS 13; since then `.automatic` almost always produces a sheet.
`.overFullScreen` has to be requested explicitly to keep the presenter visible; `.automatic` never resolves to it on its own.
On iPhone in portrait, `.formSheet` behaves like a page sheet, but the style `.automatic` resolves to is `.pageSheet`.

questions.prompt: With storyboards, where do you pass data to a segue's destination VC?
questions.explanation: `prepare(for:sender:)` receives the segue with its `destination` already instantiated, before it's shown.
whyWrong: `performSegue` starts the segue but doesn't give you access to the destination: you get the destination VC in `prepare(for:sender:)`.
In `viewDidLoad`, the destination doesn't know who opened it: the source VC has to pass it the data beforehand.
`shouldPerformSegue` only decides **whether** to perform the segue; the destination isn't instantiated yet at that point.

questions.prompt: A pushes B. To show "List" as the back button title in B, where do you set it?
questions.explanation: The back button represents the VC you go back to, so it reads the previous VC's `navigationItem`.
whyWrong: It seems logical, but the back button shown in B represents A, the VC you return to: UIKit reads A's `navigationItem`.
Replacing the `leftBarButtonItem` removes the system back button and the swipe gesture: that's not how you change just the title.
`topItem` changes as you push: relying on it is fragile, and the back title still has to be set on A's `navigationItem`.

questions.prompt: What's the main difference between `.overFullScreen` and `.fullScreen`?
options: `.overFullScreen` leaves the presenter's view in the hierarchy
questions.explanation: With `.fullScreen`, UIKit removes the underlying view once the transition ends; with `.overFullScreen`, it stays visible beneath transparent content.
whyWrong: Swipe-to-dismiss applies to sheets (`.pageSheet`/`.formSheet`): neither full-screen style offers it.
It's the other way around: `.fullScreen` removes the presenter's view, so behind transparent content you'd see black.
They're not aliases: `.fullScreen` removes the underlying view at the end of the transition, `.overFullScreen` leaves it in the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't this code compile?
options: `weak` can't be used on optional properties
questions.explanation: `weak` applies only to reference types: the protocol must be declared `: AnyObject` to use it.
whyWrong: `weak` is designed precisely for optionals: a weak reference must be able to become `nil`, so it has to be optional.
`unowned` isn't required, and it's actually riskier for a delegate: if the object goes away, accessing it crashes.
`@objc` is only needed for optional methods or Objective-C interop; the compile error comes from `weak` on a protocol that isn't class-bound.

questions.prompt: In a coordinator architecture, the user goes back with the system back button and the child coordinator stays in memory. How do you intercept it?
questions.explanation: In `didShow`, you compare the `transitionCoordinator`'s source VC against the stack: if it's gone, the flow is over and you remove the child.
whyWrong: A coordinator usually isn't a `UIViewController`, so it doesn't receive callbacks like `viewWillDisappear`.
The navigation controller stays alive during the pop, so its `deinit` never fires: it won't tell you a single flow has ended.
You can't reliably override a class method in an extension; and the system back action doesn't go through your code anyway.

questions.prompt: VC B, presented modally by A, calls `dismiss(animated: true)` on itself. What happens?
options: A is dismissed along with B
UIKit forwards the request to A and B is dismissed
Crash from calling it on the wrong VC
questions.explanation: If the VC isn't presenting anything, `dismiss` is forwarded to the presenting view controller.
whyWrong: Not so: called on B, `dismiss` is forwarded to the presenting view controller, which dismisses B.
A isn't dismissed: A is the presenter and stays; what gets removed is the presented VC, B.
No crash: UIKit handles the call by forwarding it to the presenting view controller, a very common use case.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run these two lines back to back in a VC that isn't presenting anything?
questions.code:
present(alertA, animated: true)
present(alertB, animated: true)
options: Only `alertA` appears; B logs a warning in the console
Both appear, B on top of A
questions.explanation: A VC can present only one VC at a time: the second `present` fails with an "already presenting" warning.
whyWrong: A VC can present only one VC at a time: to stack them, B would have to be presented **by** `alertA`, not by the same VC.
UIKit doesn't replace the current presentation: the second `present` is rejected with a warning.
No exception is thrown: the second `present` fails and UIKit just prints an "already presenting" warning.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent swipe-to-dismiss on a sheet that contains an unsaved form?
questions.explanation: `isModalInPresentation` blocks interactive dismissal; with the presentation delegate you can also ask for confirmation.
whyWrong: `.formSheet` can be swiped away too: changing the style doesn't block interactive dismissal.
Disabling interaction makes the form unusable and doesn't stop the swipe gesture, which the presentation handles.
Swipe-to-dismiss doesn't go through your `dismiss` override: the presentation controller handles interactive dismissal.

questions.prompt: Which API enables dependency injection via init for a VC defined in a storyboard?
questions.explanation: Since iOS 13, the `creator` closure receives the `NSCoder` and lets you call an `init?(coder:...)` with dependencies.
whyWrong: `instantiateInitialViewController()` without `creator` uses the standard `init?(coder:)`: you can't pass dependencies to the init.
In `prepare(for:sender:)`, the destination has already been created: you can assign properties, but you can't call a custom `init`.
`UINib` loads a nib, not a storyboard scene, and offers no way to inject dependencies into the init.

topics.title: Events and Gestures
topics.summary: Responder chain, hit-testing, gesture recognizers, target-action, and UIControl.

lesson.heading: Responder chain
lesson.body:
Every `UIView`, `UIViewController`, `UIWindow`, and `UIApplication` is a `UIResponder`. An unhandled event travels up the chain via `next`: view → superview (or the VC, if the view is its root view) → … → window → application → app delegate.

The **first responder** receives keyboard events and `nil`-targeted actions. To dismiss the keyboard from anywhere, use `view.endEditing(true)` or send a `resignFirstResponder` action with a `nil` target.
lesson.code:
UIApplication.shared.sendAction(
    #selector(UIResponder.resignFirstResponder),
    to: nil, from: nil, for: nil)

lesson.heading: Hit-testing
lesson.body:
To find the touched view, UIKit calls `hitTest(_:with:)` on the window, which recurses into subviews **in reverse order** (topmost first) using `point(inside:with:)`. Views with `isHidden`, `isUserInteractionEnabled = false`, or `alpha < 0.01` are skipped.

A subview that extends outside its superview's `bounds` is visible (if `clipsToBounds` is `false`) but not tappable, because the superview fails the test. Overriding `point(inside:with:)` lets you enlarge the tap area.

lesson.heading: Gesture recognizers
lesson.body:
Gesture recognizers receive touches **before** the view: once they recognize, by default (`cancelsTouchesInView = true`) they send `touchesCancelled` to the view. They're either discrete (tap) or continuous (pan, pinch), with `.began`, `.changed`, and `.ended` states.

To resolve conflicts, use `require(toFail:)` or the delegate's `gestureRecognizer(_:shouldRecognizeSimultaneouslyWith:)`. Remember that `UIImageView` and `UILabel` have `isUserInteractionEnabled = false` by default.
lesson.code:
singleTap.require(toFail: doubleTap)
imageView.isUserInteractionEnabled = true
imageView.addGestureRecognizer(singleTap)

lesson.heading: Target-action and UIControl
lesson.body:
`UIControl` (buttons, switches, sliders) sends actions for events like `.touchUpInside` and `.valueChanged`. With `addTarget(_:action:for:)`, the target **isn't retained**; since iOS 14 you can use closure-based `UIAction`s, which do retain whatever they capture.

If you pass `nil` as the target, the action travels the responder chain starting from the first responder. In custom controls, call `sendActions(for:)` to notify targets.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Classic question: **"How does UIKit figure out which view received a touch?"** Short answer: top-down hit-testing with `hitTest` and `point(inside:)`, skipping hidden, transparent, or non-interactive views; then, if the event isn't handled, it travels up the responder chain. Wrap up with a practical case: a button outside its superview's bounds, or an enlarged tap area.

questions.prompt: You add a `UITapGestureRecognizer` to a `UIImageView`, but the tap is never recognized. Most likely cause?
options: The target must be set to `nil`
questions.explanation: `UIImageView` and `UILabel` disable interaction by default, so hit-testing skips them.
whyWrong: Image views support gestures like any `UIView`; the problem is that interaction is disabled by default.
`cancelsTouchesInView` decides whether touches to the view get canceled, but it doesn't deliver touches to a view excluded from hit-testing.
A `nil` target doesn't enable anything: the recognizer never gets the touches at all, because hit-testing skips the image view.

questions.prompt: A button extends outside its superview's bounds (`clipsToBounds = false`). The outer part is visible but doesn't respond. Why?
options: The superview fails `point(inside:with:)` and hit-testing stops there
Buttons outside the bounds get disabled
The button must be brought forward with `bringSubviewToFront`
questions.explanation: Hit-testing only descends into views that contain the point: if the superview says no, its subviews are never examined.
whyWrong: UIKit doesn't disable anything: the button is enabled, but hit-testing never gets to it because the superview rejects the point.
`masksToBounds = true` would clip the outer part away: it would make it invisible, not tappable.
Bringing the button forward changes the order among siblings, but doesn't fix the fact that the point is outside the superview.

questions.prompt: Which of these views still receives touches during hit-testing?
questions.explanation: A transparent background doesn't matter: only hidden views, views with alpha below 0.01, or non-interactive views are excluded.
whyWrong: It seems visible to hit-testing, but with alpha below **0.01** the view is excluded: 0.005 is under the threshold.
Views with `isHidden = true` are skipped by hit-testing, so they don't receive touches.
`isUserInteractionEnabled = false` is exactly the flag that excludes the view (and its subviews) from hit-testing.

questions.prompt: Which `UIControl.Event` do you use for the standard tap on a `UIButton`?
questions.explanation: The action fires when the finger lifts inside the button, so the user can cancel by dragging out.
whyWrong: `.touchDown` fires as soon as the finger touches down: it doesn't let the user cancel by dragging out, so it's not the standard tap.
`.valueChanged` is for controls with a value, like `UISwitch` or `UISlider`, not for a button tap.
`.primaryActionTriggered` isn't limited to iPad, but the standard tap event on `UIButton` is still `.touchUpInside`.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code when the button is tapped?
options: The action travels up the responder chain to whoever implements it
questions.explanation: With a `nil` target, UIKit looks for the first responder in the chain that responds to the selector (a nil-targeted action).
whyWrong: A `nil` target is legal and intentional: it triggers a nil-targeted action, which searches the responder chain for a recipient.
Something does happen: UIKit walks up the responder chain and calls `copy(_:)` on the first responder that implements it.
`UIApplication` is just one of the last links: the search starts at the first responder and stops at the first one that responds.

questions.prompt: Two subviews overlap. You tap in the shared area: which one receives the touch?
questions.code:
container.addSubview(viewA)
container.addSubview(viewB)   // same frame as viewA
options: `viewB`, because it's on top and gets tested first
`container`, because the subviews cancel each other out
questions.explanation: `hitTest` walks subviews in reverse order: the last one added is the topmost and wins.
whyWrong: Insertion order matters the other way around: the first one added sits underneath, and `hitTest` checks the last subview first.
Hit-testing returns **a single** view: the first one that contains the point, walking subviews from top to bottom.
Subviews don't cancel each other out: a view containing the point is found, and the container only gets the touch if none accepts it.

questions.prompt: A view has both a single tap and a double tap. On a double tap, the single tap fires too. How do you fix it?
questions.explanation: The single tap waits for the double tap to fail before recognizing, at the cost of a small delay.
whyWrong: It's backwards: this way the double tap waits for the single tap, which still fires on the first tap.
`cancelsTouchesInView` is about touches forwarded to the view, not about two recognizers competing.
`numberOfTouchesRequired` counts **fingers**, not taps: the single tap would then require two fingers at once.

questions.prompt: You add a tap gesture to the view containing a `UITableView` to dismiss the keyboard. Now `didSelectRowAt` is never called. Why?
options: Table views don't receive touches when there's a gesture
The tap gesture becomes the first responder
`cancelsTouchesInView` is `true` and cancels the table's touches
questions.explanation: When the recognizer recognizes, the view receives `touchesCancelled`; setting `cancelsTouchesInView = false` makes selection work again.
whyWrong: Table views receive touches normally; the point is that the recognizer, when it recognizes, cancels the touches meant for the table.
A gesture recognizer isn't a responder and never becomes first responder: the problem is `cancelsTouchesInView`.
`endEditing` just dismisses the keyboard: it doesn't affect table selection, which is being canceled by the recognizer.

questions.prompt: What is the `next` responder of a `UIViewController`'s root view?
questions.explanation: The root view forwards to its VC; from the VC, the chain continues to the view's superview or the parent.
whyWrong: The window comes later in the chain: before the superview, the root view goes through its view controller.
`UIApplication` is near the end of the chain: from the root view you first go to the VC, then superview, window, and app.
The root view forwards to the VC that owns it; only from the VC can the chain move up to a container, like the navigation controller.

questions.prompt: Which statement about memory in target-action is correct?
options: `addTarget` doesn't retain the target; `UIAction` closures do
questions.explanation: The control doesn't hold on to the target, but a `UIAction` closure that captures `self` strongly can create a retain cycle.
whyWrong: The control doesn't hold on to the target: that's why, if the target is deallocated, the action simply stops being sent.
The `UIAction` closure is retained by the control: if it captures `self` strongly, it can create a retain cycle.
`UIAction` doesn't weaken anything on its own: captures are strong by default, and it's up to you to write `[weak self]`.

topics.title: Threading and UI
topics.summary: Main thread, GCD, OperationQueue, DispatchGroup, and race conditions.

lesson.heading: The main thread rule
lesson.body:
UIKit isn't thread-safe: nearly all `UIView` and `UIViewController` APIs must be used **only from the main thread**, which also runs the rendering and event run loop. With Swift Concurrency these classes are annotated `@MainActor`, and Xcode's **Main Thread Checker** flags violations at runtime.

Heavy work (networking, parsing, image decoding) belongs in the background; then you hop back to main to update the UI.

lesson.heading: Grand Central Dispatch
lesson.body:
GCD offers **serial** queues (one task at a time, FIFO) and **concurrent** queues: `DispatchQueue.main` is serial, the `global(qos:)` queues are concurrent. `async` enqueues and returns immediately; `sync` blocks the caller until the task finishes.

Calling `DispatchQueue.main.sync` from the main thread causes a **deadlock** (libdispatch detects it and crashes). For the reader/writer pattern, use a custom concurrent queue with `.barrier` on writes: on global queues, the barrier has no effect.

lesson.heading: OperationQueue
lesson.body:
`OperationQueue` sits one level above GCD: `Operation`s support **dependencies** (`addDependency`), **cancellation** (`cancel()` and checking `isCancelled`), priorities, and `maxConcurrentOperationCount` to limit parallelism.

It's handy for download or processing pipelines you need to be able to cancel, for example when a cell scrolls off screen.

lesson.heading: DispatchGroup
lesson.body:
`DispatchGroup` coordinates multiple async tasks: `enter()` before each one, `leave()` when it's done (**on every path**, including errors), and `notify(queue:)` when they've all finished. `wait()` blocks the current thread: never on main.

With Swift Concurrency, you get the same result with `async let` or `withTaskGroup`.

lesson.heading: Race conditions and Swift Concurrency
lesson.body:
A **data race** happens when multiple threads access the same memory and at least one writes, without synchronization: the result is nondeterministic. You prevent it with a serial queue, a lock (`NSLock`, `OSAllocatedUnfairLock`), or an **actor**, and you catch it with the **Thread Sanitizer**.

In Swift Concurrency, a `Task {}` created from a `@MainActor` context (like a VC) inherits its isolation: the synchronous code inside it runs on the main thread.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Classic question: **"Why does the UI have to be updated on the main thread?"** Short answer: UIKit isn't thread-safe, and the main run loop handles events and rendering; updating from other threads leads to nondeterministic glitches or crashes. Then show how you get back to main (`DispatchQueue.main.async` or `@MainActor`) and how you protect shared state with serial queues or actors.

questions.prompt: Which thread does the `URLSession.shared.dataTask` completion run on?
options: On a background queue: for UI work you have to hop back to main
questions.explanation: The shared session uses a serial background delegate queue, so UI updates have to be dispatched back to main.
whyWrong: `URLSession.shared` doesn't automatically return to main: the completion runs on its background delegate queue.
`resume()` starts the task and returns immediately: the completion doesn't run on the calling thread but on the session's queue.
The session uses its own delegate queue (a serial `OperationQueue`), not a specific global queue with `.userInteractive` QoS.

questions.prompt: What happens when you run this code from the main thread?
options: Deadlock: libdispatch detects it and the app crashes
The block runs on the next run loop iteration
questions.explanation: `sync` waits for the block to finish, but the block can't start because main is busy waiting.
whyWrong: `sync` on main from main can't start: main is blocked waiting on itself, so the text never updates.
That would be the behavior of `async`: with `sync`, main stays blocked and the run loop never advances.
GCD doesn't convert `sync` to `async`: it detects the deadlock and crashes the app.

questions.prompt: What does this code print when run on the main thread?
questions.explanation: The block is enqueued on main and runs only after the current code has finished.
whyWrong: `async` doesn't run the block right away: it enqueues it on main, which is busy until the current code finishes.
The block can't jump ahead of `print("1")`, which already ran before the block was even enqueued.
Everything happens on the same serial queue, main: the order is deterministic, and the enqueued block runs last.

questions.prompt: In this code, `notify` sometimes never gets called. Why?
options: `enter` must be called inside the closure
questions.explanation: Every `enter` needs its `leave` on every path: use `defer { group.leave() }`.
whyWrong: `enter` must be called **before** starting the async work: inside the closure, the group might already look empty.
`notify` can be registered at any time; the problem is the missing `leave` on the error path.
`DispatchGroup` works just fine with closures; here it hangs only because `enter` isn't always balanced.

questions.prompt: What happens when you use `.barrier` on `DispatchQueue.global()`?
options: No barrier effect: it behaves like a regular `async`
It serializes only tasks with the same QoS
questions.explanation: Barriers only work on concurrent queues you create; global queues are shared with the system.
whyWrong: A barrier on a global queue doesn't block anything: global queues are shared with the system and ignore it.
QoS has nothing to do with barriers: on a global queue, the `.barrier` flag is simply ignored.
No crash: the flag is ignored and the block runs like a regular concurrent `async`.

questions.prompt: Why must UIKit updates happen on the main thread?
options: The main thread has more memory available
UIKit isn't thread-safe and the main run loop handles rendering
questions.explanation: Concurrent access to UIKit state produces nondeterministic glitches and crashes.
whyWrong: All threads share the same process memory: the reason is UIKit's lack of thread safety.
Technically you can allocate a view on another thread; the problem is that accessing UIKit state concurrently isn't safe.
It applies on device too: UIKit isn't thread-safe anywhere, and the Main Thread Checker flags it in both.

questions.prompt: What advantage does `OperationQueue` offer over plain GCD?
options: It runs tasks on the main thread by default
Dependencies between tasks, cancellation, and a concurrency limit
questions.explanation: `addDependency`, `cancel()`, and `maxConcurrentOperationCount` are built in, whereas with GCD you have to build them by hand.
whyWrong: `OperationQueue` is built on top of GCD and adds overhead: the advantage is in features, not speed.
An `OperationQueue()` you create runs in the background; only `OperationQueue.main` uses the main thread.
No queue prevents race conditions on its own: with multiple concurrent operations you still have to synchronize shared state.

questions.prompt: What value does this code print?
questions.code:
var count = 0
DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform(iterations: 1000) { _ in
    count += 1
}
print(count)
options: A nondeterministic value, often less than 1000
questions.explanation: `count += 1` isn't atomic: concurrent reads and writes overlap (a data race).
whyWrong: It seems obvious it would reach 1000, but the iterations run in parallel and `count += 1` isn't atomic: some increments get lost.
`concurrentPerform` is synchronous: by the time `print` runs, all iterations have finished, so the value doesn't stay at 0.
In Swift 5 it compiles without errors: the compiler doesn't detect the data race, which at most shows up at runtime.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a serial queue?
options: It always runs on the main thread
It runs tasks in parallel but in order
It runs one task at a time in FIFO order
It uses a single fixed thread for the app's entire lifetime
questions.explanation: Serial means one task at a time; the underlying thread can change from one task to the next.
whyWrong: Only the main queue is tied to the main thread: serial queues you create run on background threads.
Parallel and serial are mutually exclusive: a serial queue runs one task at a time, never two at once.
GCD doesn't dedicate a fixed thread to the queue: the underlying thread can change from one task to the next.

questions.prompt: In a `UIViewController`, which thread does `heavyParse()` (a synchronous, nonisolated function) run on?
options: On the main thread: the Task inherits `@MainActor` isolation
On a background thread from the cooperative pool
On a new thread created just for it
It depends on the device's QoS
questions.explanation: A synchronous function runs on the caller's executor: to move the work off main you need `Task.detached` or a `@concurrent` function.
whyWrong: The `Task` inherits the VC's `@MainActor` isolation, and a synchronous function runs on the caller's executor: it stays on main.
`Task` doesn't create dedicated threads: it uses existing executors, and here it inherits the main actor's.
QoS affects priority, not isolation: the code runs on main because the `Task` inherits `@MainActor`.

topics.title: Architecture
topics.summary: MVC, MVVM, VIPER, coordinators, and patterns for communication between objects.

lesson.heading: MVC and Massive View Controller
lesson.body:
In Apple's MVC, the `UIViewController` mediates between model and view, but it's tightly coupled to the view (it manages its lifecycle). The risk is the **Massive View Controller**: networking, formatting, validation, navigation, and data sources all in the same file.

You slim it down with child view controllers, separate data sources, injected services, and by extracting navigation.

lesson.heading: MVVM
lesson.body:
The **ViewModel** turns model data into view-ready state (formatted strings, loading flags) and exposes inputs as methods. It doesn't import UIKit and holds no reference to the view, so you can test it with plain unit tests.

Binding is done with closures, Combine (`@Published`), or `@Observable`. Starting with iOS 26, UIKit automatically tracks `@Observable` properties read in methods like `layoutSubviews` (on iOS 18 you need an Info.plist key).

lesson.heading: VIPER and Clean Architecture
lesson.body:
VIPER splits a module into **View**, **Interactor** (business logic), **Presenter** (presentation logic), **Entity**, and **Router** (navigation). Every part talks through protocols, so everything is mockable.

The cost is a lot of boilerplate: it makes sense for large teams with independent modules and is overkill for small apps. In an interview, what matters is weighing the trade-off, not reciting the acronym.

lesson.heading: Coordinator
lesson.body:
A coordinator pulls navigation out of view controllers: the VCs (or ViewModels) signal an intent, such as "user selected", and the coordinator decides what to show. Combined with MVVM, it's called **MVVM-C**.

Benefits: reusable VCs, centralized deep links, testable flows. Be careful to manage the lifecycle of child coordinators.

lesson.heading: Communication patterns
lesson.body:
**Delegation**: one-to-one, good for several related callbacks or methods that return values. **Closures**: lightweight one-to-one, for a single callback. **NotificationCenter**: one-to-many, decoupled but loosely typed. **KVO**: observes `@objc dynamic` properties of `NSObject` subclasses. **Combine**: declarative streams, with subscriptions kept in `AnyCancellable`.

In every case, watch your memory: `weak` delegates, `[weak self]` in closures, tokens and cancellables kept alive for exactly the right amount of time.
lesson.code:
viewModel.$title
    .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)
    .sink { [weak self] in self?.titleLabel.text = $0 }
    .store(in: &cancellables)

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body: Typical question: **"Which architecture would you use, and why?"** Short answer: there's no universally right one; MVVM with coordinators is a good default for testability and separation, VIPER only if the team and domain justify the cost. Always back it up with testability, team size, and maintenance, and show you know why MVC tends to degrade.

questions.prompt: What typically causes a Massive View Controller?
options: The VC piles up networking, formatting, navigation, and data sources
Too many subviews in the hierarchy
questions.explanation: The VC becomes the default home for every responsibility because it's where model and view meet.
whyWrong: Storyboards move UI construction out of code: if anything they slim the VC down, they don't make it massive.
Lots of subviews make the hierarchy heavy, but the Massive VC problem is about the number of **responsibilities**, not views.
Auto Layout is just a layout system; the VC bloats when it piles up networking, logic, and navigation.

questions.prompt: In MVVM, which of these traits should the ViewModel have?
options: It holds a strong reference to the view
It doesn't depend on UIKit and exposes already-formatted state
questions.explanation: Without UIKit and without references to the view, the ViewModel can be tested with plain unit tests.
whyWrong: The view observes the ViewModel, not the other way around: a strong reference to the view would couple it to UIKit.
A ViewModel that subclasses `UIViewController` is just a view controller again and loses all its testability.
Constraints belong to the view: the ViewModel exposes state, it doesn't manage layout or UIKit objects.

questions.prompt: In VIPER, which component contains the business logic?
questions.explanation: The Interactor runs the use cases; the Presenter prepares data for the view, and the Router handles navigation.
whyWrong: The Presenter is the bridge: it prepares data for the view and reacts to input, but delegates use cases to the Interactor.
The Router only handles navigation between modules, not business logic.
The Entity is the data model, usually plain structs with no logic: use cases live in the Interactor.

questions.prompt: You need to notify several independent screens that the user logged out. Which mechanism fits best?
questions.explanation: Delegates and closures are one-to-one; `NotificationCenter` is designed for one-to-many broadcasts.
whyWrong: A delegate connects an object to **a single** recipient: notifying many screens would take many delegates.
A callback closure is one-to-one like a delegate: it's not suited to broadcasting to independent screens.
`UIApplication` doesn't expose a logout property to observe, and KVO requires `@objc dynamic`: it's not the right tool.

questions.prompt: When is a delegate preferable to a closure?
options: When you need a single callback
With several related callbacks or methods that return values
questions.explanation: That's the `UITableViewDataSource` model: a protocol groups many interactions under a clear contract.
whyWrong: With a single callback a closure is usually simpler and more readable: a delegate pays off with many related callbacks.
Neither delegates nor closures are meant for many recipients: for broadcasting there's `NotificationCenter`.
Closures don't always win: with many related methods, or methods that return values, a protocol is clearer.

questions.prompt: What do you need to observe a property of your own Swift class with KVO?
options: An `NSObject` subclass and an `@objc dynamic` property
